data.title: Why Jensen Huang and Nvidia matter so much to markets
data.description:
The decision by Nvidia’s board of directors to restore Jensen Huang as chief executive on Nov 23 after President Donald Trump pressed for the move speaks to the enormous impact both of Huang on the company and of the company on the larger stock market.

The sharp decline in Nvidia’s stock price that began after news emerged that Huang had had an affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Chinese intelligence erased more than US$2 trillion (S$2.6 trillion) dollars of value from the stock market, which Trump has long cited as a metric for his presidency.

It was Huang’s decision to pivot Nvidia’s focus from graphics chips for gaming to the artificial intelligence “accelerators” that made it one the world’s biggest companies by market value.

At its peak, in early October, Nvidia’s market capitalisation totalled around US$5.8 trillion, a figure larger than the national economic output of Germany.

Huang’s globetrotting lobbying helped to maintain its dominant position.

Hence the sharp sell-off of Nvidia’s shares that began when the espionage scandal first raised questions about his future at the company and continued after he resigned on Nov 12.

The trend began to reverse after the leather-jacketed, celebrity co-founder’s reinstatement as CEO. 

Here is why the stakes in this saga have been so high.

Market titan

On Nov 30, 2022, a then little-known company called OpenAI released a chatbot called ChatGPT, triggering an explosion in demand for a type of computing chip that Nvidia was uniquely well-placed to provide. Over the next few years, Nvidia’s share price rose fourteenfold before peaking in early October.

The company witnessed soaring demand from data-centre customers, including Alphabet, Amazon.com and Microsoft. In mid-2024, it overtook all three by market capitalisation for the first time. In 2025, Nvidia became the first company to surpass both US$4 trillion and US$5 trillion in market value. 

By early October, it was closing in on the US$6 trillion mark. However, investors were becoming increasingly skittish over frothy AI stock valuations and an industry borrowing spree, and Nvidia fell behind Apple as the world’s biggest company. 

Following the revelations about Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese agent, reports of an affair with another woman who worked for him, and his resignation, Nvidia’s valuation fell to about US$3 trillion as at Nov 20, the Friday before Huang was reinstated.

The news that he had returned to the company sent the valuation shooting back upwards.

Chip supremacy

Nvidia accounts for an overwhelming share of sales of the advanced chips that process AI tasks.

Its dominance partly reflects a substantial head start: Years before AI really took off, the company was investing in ways to sell its graphics processing units for uses beyond gaming.

It maintained that lead by rolling out new designs every year.

Its size and purchasing power kept it ahead of the game, making it harder for smaller rivals to keep up. 

The leadership turmoil came at an especially bad time.

Nvidia’s rivals, and even some of its customers, are working hard to develop competitive AI chips.

A raft of start-ups are raising billions of dollars from investors keen to back the next breakthrough.

Competition is also intensifying in China, where the company is prevented by US export controls from selling its most advanced products.

Companies such as Huawei Technologies – blacklisted in the US – are making rapid strides in developing homegrown AI chips, Nvidia has said. 

AI finance linchpin

Since 2024, Nvidia has become not just a supplier to the AI industry but also one of its key financial backers.

It has invested heavily in leading AI platform developers, including OpenAI, Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Mistral of France, as well as companies building AI data centres.

It is a symbiotic relationship: Nvidia helps to finance the expansion of AI infrastructure, stoking demand for Nvidia’s chips. 

Portfolio Dominance

Until mid-2020, Nvidia’s market capitalisation represented less than 1% of the total value of all the companies tracked in the S&P 500 index, the standard benchmark for the US stock market.

For much of the past two years, Nvidia’s share hovered around 8%, the largest slice of any company.

In the wake of Huang’s troubles, Nvidia’s share of the total value fell to 5% as at Nov. 20.

Because of the company’s weight, its health can significantly affect the overall value of the S&P 500, to which enormous amounts of money are tied.

Some US$20 trillion in assets is either indexed or benchmarked to it, according to S&P Global. These are held largely through retirement funds, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds.

Key-man risk

Huang has been known for his exacting management style at Nvidia, even in an industry full of domineering CEOs who obsess over details.

In his previous role as CEO, every major decision flowed through him, and he weighed in on even the most minute aspects of the business.

Huang had about 60 people reporting to him directly, far more than the average tech leader.

They sent him e-mails with “top five things” that he read and responded to at all hours.

The scandals involving Huang underscored Nvidia’s “key-man” risk: The 63-year-old executive was seen as inseparable from the company’s success.

Huang’s exit had put Nvidia in an unusually vulnerable position for a company of its size: There was no one designated to replace him. BLOOMBERG

data.title: DeepSeek founder worth US$55 billion after latest fundraising
data.description:
HANGZHOU – DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng’s fortune climbed to US$55 billion (S$71 billion) after the Chinese artificial intelligence start-up completed its latest fundraising, drawing investment from industrial tycoons and cementing his status as the world’s richest creator of AI models.

Liang’s stake in the Hangzhou-based firm fell to 67.4% from 81.65% in June, according to registry filings.

DeepSeek’s implied valuation is US$86 billion, based on the roughly 100 billion yuan (S$19 billion) that the firm recently raised, according to people familiar with the matter, and calculations by the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Liang’s net worth has more than tripled from earlier in 2026, according to the wealth index.

The latest numbers show Liang’s growing financial power, even as cracks emerge in the AI boom that on Nov 20 pushed the S&P 500 into a correction.

They also underscore how China’s richest are backing DeepSeek, which has evolved from a hedge fund side project into a centerpiece of the country’s AI ambitions.

The firm is preparing for a potential initial public offering in 2027.

The surge means that Liang, born in 1985, has put more distance between his own wealth and that of rival US-based founders.

His fortune is more than double that of OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, worth about US$25.5 billion as at Nov 20.

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei was worth about US$22 billion at the end of last week following the firm’s listing.

That gap is largely because Liang still controls more than two-thirds of DeepSeek, whereas the others hold smaller stakes in their companies.

DeepSeek did not respond to requests for comment. 

Records from data aggregator Qichacha also disclosed mostly new personal stakes held by at least five other Chinese billionaires in the AI firm.

Among the billionaire backers of DeepSeek are Contemporary Amperex Technology founder Robin Zeng, taking a new 0.18% personal stake valued at US$154.6 million alongside the battery giant’s institutional investment.

Nongfu Spring founder Zhong Shanshan, who first invested in DeepSeek’s previous funding round, holds a 0.08% stake now worth US$70.6 million.

Liang founded DeepSeek in 2023 as an offshoot of the AI research unit inside Zhejiang High-Flyer Asset Management, the quantitative hedge fund he co-founded with two university classmates after they began trading during the global financial crisis. BLOOMBERG

data.title: US Fed has ‘work to do’ to lower inflation, Williams says
data.description:
NEW YORK - New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Nov 23 that persistently high inflation continues to point the US central bank toward tighter monetary policy.

“We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis,” Williams said in remarks prepared for delivery to an event at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York City.

“There is still work to do to get that done.”

Williams said inflation is “too high” and that it must be lowered back to the Fed’s target “in a timely manner and on a sustained basis”.

He noted that he will continue to assess incoming data to decide what action the central bank should take at its Dec 8-9 policy meeting.

Financial markets broadly expect the Fed to raise its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point in December from the current 3.75%-4.00% range, with more increases to come in 2027.

The Fed last raised rates in September as part of an effort to curb inflation, which has been above the 2% target for more than five years.

Central bank officials worry that, if this situation persists, the public could lose confidence that inflation will return to that level.

Williams was speaking the same day as a sharp stock market rally, triggered by chipmaker Nvidia’s announcement that it was reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, after US President Donald Trump urged it to do so.

Investors’ reaction highlighted the importance of AI companies in driving the markets.

Some observers had wondered in recent days whether sharp stock losses might deter the Fed from raising rates.

In his remarks, Williams said that he expects inflation to end the year at 3.5% and to moderate to just above 2% in 2027 before easing to the target in 2028.

He also noted that risks to inflation continue to be skewed to the upside.

Williams noted that among the key drivers of high price pressures, energy prices remain elevated and the outlook on that front is uncertain.

He added that “although the effects of tariffs, geopolitical conflicts, and the AI surge are showing up in prices of certain categories of goods, there is little evidence of these spilling over significantly into broader and more persistent inflation”.

Williams also said the economy is showing strength and resilience and should grow by 2.75% in both 2026 and 2027.

He added that the job market has been showing stability, and the current 4.1% unemployment rate should fall to around 4% in 2027. REUTERS

data.title: US stocks surge as Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO
data.description:
US stocks surged on Nov 23, led by a big jump in the Nasdaq as Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO drove investors back into AI-related shares after last week’s rout.

Nvidia’s shares shot up as much as 36.6% after the board returned Huang. He had resigned from the company on Nov 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

US President Donald Trump said he secured a deal with Nvidia’s board to bring back Huang as CEO. Nvidia is widely seen as a cornerstone of the AI trade.

The news helped Wall Street recover from last week’s sharp selloff. On Nov 20, the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections as worries mounted about the AI trade.

The Nasdaq-100 added more than US$2 trillion (S$2.3 trillion) in market value on Nov 23, while the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 had their biggest daily gains since the market surged after Trump paused his “Liberation Day” tariff package in April 2025.

“The thought had been, and it’s being borne out today, that Jensen Huang is uniquely important to Nvidia and to the AI trade,” said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments.

Still, he said, “you have one issue that is resolved – and it’s a biggie – but you still have to see how the rest of things play out.”

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 gained 328.45 points, or 4.75%, to end at 7,238.84 points, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 1,463.21 points, or 6.47%, to 24,080.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,452.56 points, or 3.02%, to 49,599.89.

Before Nov 23, the Nasdaq had come close to entering a bear market as investors worried about the heavy borrowing underpinning AI investment and questioned whether the sector could deliver sufficient returns. Fears of political scrutiny also mounted after Democrats swept the US midterm elections.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index and S&P 500 information technology sector both were sharply higher on Monday, along with megacap stocks such as Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet.

Also climbing were neocloud and data centre companies, which had come under sharp selling pressure following Huang’s abrupt exit. Other sectors also rose, with energy being the only group in negative territory.

“We don’t think the rebound has run its course, and at these levels, it’s not too late to gradually add back technology exposure,” said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Ahead this week is Nov 25’s personal consumption expenditures report, which could give clues about the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy outlook. REUTERS

data.title: How cash-flow planning and technology can help SMEs turn opportunities into growth
data.description:
After months of pitching, your business has landed its biggest client project of the year.

But delivering it means spending before getting paid: materials have to be ordered, subcontractors engaged and employees paid, while the customer may not settle the bill until 30 or 60 days after the work is completed and invoiced.

For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), a healthy order book does not always translate into cash available to meet immediate expenses.

The challenge of turning business opportunities into growth was among the themes explored at Singtel and GXS Business Banking’s Good Business Starts With Good Flow event.

Guests included filmmaker Annette Lee, who shared her experiences of pursuing opportunities for growth, as well as fengshui master Mark Tan, who spoke about creating the conditions for success.  

Business owners who attended the event heard from their fellow entrepreneurs and industry experts on the different aspects of business “flow”, from securing funding to improving operations and building connections.

The common thread was that SMEs need both the financial capacity to act on opportunities and the operational capacity to deliver on them.  

This is where GXS Business Banking and Singtel play complementary roles.

GXS Business Banking provides tailored business loans – from unsecured working capital to up to $5 million in property-backed financing – while Singtel offers practical AI and digital solutions to help businesses streamline operations, improve productivity and manage growing workloads.

Managing cash flow as your business grows 

Working capital financing can be a boon for companies facing cash flow pressures as they grow. Rather than getting caught off guard by a shortfall, planning ahead can help owners work out how much funding they may need, when they need it and how repayments align with incoming payments.

GXS Business Banking offers financing solutions for different stages of a company’s growth cycle. Purchase Order Financing can help eligible SMEs cover costs at the start of a project, while Invoice Financing can provide earlier access to cash after an invoice has been issued.

The type of financing needed can therefore change as a project progresses – from funding the work upfront to keeping cash available while waiting for payment.

GXS Business Banking financing solutions can help businesses manage everyday expenses while retaining the flexibility to pursue new business opportunities.

Using technology to create room for growth

Access to financing is one part of preparing for growth. But for SMEs with lean teams, lengthy application processes and labour-intensive operations can also make it harder to act quickly on new opportunities.

Technology can help businesses address both.

At GXS Business Banking, technology and data are used to streamline the financing process. Instead of relying solely on credit bureau information, its credit assessment models also consider data such as transaction flows and invoicing patterns.

AI-enabled tools help automate parts of the onboarding and credit assessment process.

By reducing manual paperwork and processing, this approach can make applying for financing more straightforward and help eligible SMEs access working capital sooner.

Technology can also help businesses make better use of their resources once funding is in place.

As they grow, SMEs may want to use artificial intelligence (AI) to achieve the same outcomes as larger companies – better customer service, greater productivity and lower costs – but often have less time, specialist expertise and budget to implement such tools.

Singtel’s Stack-EZ, an AI, digital and cloud solutions portfolio under its International Digital Services business, aims to simplify digital adoption by bringing together ready-to-deploy solutions and implementation support.

For example, Stack-EZ’s AI solutions help businesses automate customer interactions, streamline workflows and improve operational efficiency, while its cloud solutions provide scalable infrastructure to support business growth.

Singtel supports businesses throughout their digitalisation journey, from solution implementation and onboarding to ongoing assistance.

By automating repetitive tasks and workflows, these solutions can free employees to focus on customer service, business development and work that requires human judgement.

Agentic AI can go beyond answering enquiries by carrying out routine tasks and coordinating parts of a workflow, potentially helping small teams manage growing workloads more consistently.

Adopting new technology, however, may require upfront investment before productivity gains materialise. GXS Business Banking’s financing solutions can support eligible investments, while Singtel’s digital solutions can help businesses improve their operations. To explore Singtel’s AI, digital and cloud solutions, visit stackez.com.

For SMEs, being ready for growth means having both the financial resources and the operational capacity to deliver – so that when the next big order arrives, they are better placed to take it on.

data.title: Stocks climb as Huang’s stunning return to Nvidia lifts optimism
data.description:
LONDON – Shares in AI chip behemoth Nvidia rocketed almost 30% higher on Nov 23 after the shock reinstatement of its chief executive officer Jensen Huang, which sparked a recovery after a technology-led rout last week.

Major indices dived between 7% and 10% last week but investors were galvanised on the news of Huang’s return, less than two weeks after he resigned over an alleged Chinese spy scandal and an affair with an employee.

“Jensen Huang is the AI comeback kid,” said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

But “that doesn’t mean the volatility is over”, she said.

She added: “The company is still under scrutiny from investigators, from the FBI to Capitol Hill, over the spy scandal that brought him down.”

US President Donald Trump, who pressed for Huang’s reinstatement, hailed the decision, saying the government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security”.

“The Nvidia board of directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO,” Trump wrote on social media.

The news promptly hoisted the tech-heavy Nasdaq more than 6% while the DOW added 2.6% and the broader-based S&P 500 rose 4.5% minutes into the session.

European markets saw smaller gains of around 1.5%, following heavy selling of tech stocks in Asia.

Seoul, home to chip giants SK hynix and Samsung, slid by more than 3%.

“These are not peripheral players in the AI boom but two of its most important semiconductor suppliers,” said Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.

“Their continued weakness suggests investors are still more interested in reducing exposure than celebrating a few hours of improved sentiment in US futures,” he said.

The losses have led authorities in some countries to introduce measures aimed at minimising the negative impact.

Taiwan is making it harder to short stocks, or betting that prices will fall, while China made it easier to borrow money to buy them and South Korea eyed a stabilisation fund not used since the global financial crisis. AFP

data.title: OCBC names Ang Eng Siong as global corporate banking head in rejig of wholesale banking business
data.description:
SINGAPORE – OCBC has appointed Ang Eng Siong, the current chief executive of OCBC China, as its new head of global corporate banking from Jan 1, 2027.

The appointment comes as the bank reorganises its wholesale banking business into three divisions, to sharpen its focus when serving large corporations, multinational companies, financial institutions, public sector and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), it said on Nov 23.

“All companies, including banks, are navigating a volatile and fast-evolving environment,” said OCBC group CEO Tan Teck Long.

“A transformational reorganisation of our wholesale banking business will position us even better to elevate how we serve customers, and meet both the challenges and opportunities facing us.”

Under the new structure, Ang will lead what OCBC calls “GWB 1”, focusing on scaling the large corporate segment in its core markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Greater China – as well as its overseas branches.

Meanwhile, current global corporate banking head Elaine Lam will take charge of “GWB 3”, which covers global institutional, investment and transaction banking.

Tan said GWB 3 will sharpen the bank’s focus on products and structured solutions to support large corporates and SMEs globally.

“This new division,” OCBC said, “will strengthen the products and solutions capabilities in transaction banking, investment banking, structured finance and financial institutions group under an expanded mandate, and develop new growth platforms”.

GWB 3 will also seek to deepen cross-selling opportunities through greater global institutional and industry coverage, while “driving origination and strategic solutioning”.

Lam will lead OCBC’s expansion into the large alternative investment firms, asset managers, global institutions and sponsors space, the bank said.

Ang joined OCBC in July 2009 as a management associate, and moved to China in 2015 to join the corporate banking team. He was appointed CEO of OCBC China in 2023 and will remain in the role until a successor is appointed.

During his tenure, he drove OCBC China’s “strategic repositioning” around Greater China-Asean connectivity, cross-border wealth, differentiated customer propositions, as well as artificial intelligence and digital transformation, the bank said.

Lam, who had been head of global corporate banking since 2016, grew the bank’s corporate banking franchise in specialised and high-growth sectors, strengthened cross-selling and built a diversified business across OCBC’s core markets and overseas branches.

She joined OCBC in 2001 as a relationship manager.

“GWB 2”, which represents the current global commercial banking arm, will continue to be led by Elaine Heng, who will focus on the SME segment.

Shares of OCBC closed 0.5% or $0.13 lower at $26.41 on Nov 23, before the announcement. THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: Winding-up bid adds to SGX-listed ASA’s woes amid trading suspension
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Catalist-listed Advanced Systems Automation (ASA) is facing a winding-up application over a disputed claim of more than $643,000, adding to the troubles of a company whose shares have been suspended from trading amid concerns over its financial health.

ASA, which manufactures automated equipment used in semiconductor production, is being pursued by its former continuing sponsor and financial adviser Zico Capital over allegedly unpaid fees.

A continuing sponsor helps companies listed on the Singapore Exchange’s (SGX) Catalist board comply with listing requirements.

Zico filed the winding-up application in the High Court on Nov 3, with a hearing scheduled for Dec 4.

If granted, the application could result in ASA being liquidated and its assets used to repay creditors.

Dispute dates back to March

The legal dispute dates back to March, when ASA received a demand from Zico for $627,708, including interest, for fees for continuing sponsorship services and financial advisory work, including ASA’s acquisition of LSO Organization Holdings, as well as interest.

By the time Zico’s statutory demand was served on ASA on July 1, the amount had risen to $643,534.82.

ASA disputed the claim and on July 22 filed a separate High Court lawsuit seeking approximately $6.79 million plus interest, alleging that Zico breached its duties as financial adviser, resulting in losses.

It also attempted to stop Zico from commencing winding-up proceedings, but the High Court dismissed its application for an injunction on Sept 7 and ordered it to pay $18,000 in legal costs.

The decision did not resolve ASA’s $6.79 million claim and, on the High Court’s order, the company has set aside $42,000 as security for Zico’s potental legal costs held in ASA’s lawyer’s stakeholder account.

Trading suspension

ASA has been grappling with questions over its ability to remain in business.

For the financial year ended Dec 31, 2025, ASA’s group recorded a net loss of $5.55 million, while the company on a standalone basis incurred a larger loss of $10.96 million.

The group also had net current liabilities of $8.16 million, meaning its short-term liabilities exceeded its short-term assets.

Its auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion on its 2025 financial statements, saying they could not obtain sufficient evidence to determine whether it was appropriate to prepare the accounts on the assumption that the company could continue operating.

Despite its financial difficulties, ASA maintained in its Nov 6 announcement that it could continue operating, saying receipts from its business activities were helping it meet its financial obligations.

It also said it was discussing structured repayment arrangements with several major creditors.

However, on Nov 13, SGX RegCo directed that an earlier trading halt be converted into a suspension with immediate effect.

The regulator said that, after reviewing the company’s information and responses and considering its continuing sponsor’s assessment, ASA had been unable to demonstrate to the exchange and its shareholders that it could continue operating as a going concern.

ASA is required to provide monthly updates on the winding-up proceedings and its financial position.

Its current continuing sponsor, Asian Corporate Advisors, has also given notice to terminate its appointment by Jan 26, 2027, unless an earlier date is agreed on.

Under Catalist rules, companies without a continuing sponsor will have their shares suspended from trading and may be delisted if they remain without one for more than three consecutive months.

data.title: Russia eyes Singapore to deepen business ties across ASEAN despite ongoing sanctions
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Russia expects Singapore’s 2027 ASEAN chairmanship to inject fresh momentum into business ties with the Republic and the region, seeing opportunities in technology, logistics and financial infrastructure even as sanctions continue to complicate trade and investment.

Singapore is a key gateway for Russian companies seeking to expand into South-East Asia, said Alexander Stuglev, chairman and director of Russia’s Roscongress Foundation, which promotes economic development, investment and international cooperation.

Citing digital technology as an example, Stuglev said Russian companies have accumulated deep experience in cybersecurity, Internet of Things applications and platform solutions.

“This experience can be adapted to the Singaporean market and then scaled across the Asia-Pacific,” he said.

The potential for partnerships here and the region is also seen in areas such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, transport connectivity and energy, Stuglev said.

“Singapore is a special case for us. We see it as a hub through which Russian companies, together with local partners, enter the entire region,” he told The Straits Times in an interview late Nov 20.

The state-backed Roscongress Foundation organises some of Russia’s largest business events, including the St Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF) and the Eastern Economic Forum. 

It runs around 150 events a year with participants from more than 200 countries and territories, and has in recent years held business events across the region, including in Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.  

Stuglev was in Singapore to attend the Russia–Singapore Business Dialogue on Nov 19 to 20, held at the Four Seasons.

The event brought together companies from Russia, Singapore and the region to explore cooperation in artificial intelligence and digital technology, finance, education, industrial automation and additive manufacturing. 

Singapore chairing ASEAN in 2027 is an opportunity to build on existing business links.

In Russia for an ASEAN-Russia summit in June, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore looked forward to practical cooperation between the grouping and Russia during its chairmanship.

“For us, this is an important signal. Russia sees ASEAN as an equal dialogue partner, and the change of chair can give a new (impetus) to the groundwork already laid,” Stuglev said.

He identified potential collaboration in financial infrastructure and new payment systems, in information technology, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, the Internet of Things and platform solutions, as well as in transport and logistics connectivity, including the Northern Sea Route, in energy and deep processing of raw materials. 

But the opportunities come against a backdrop of financial and export restrictions imposed by the international community on Russia following its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which continue to constrain commercial dealings.

On March 5, 2022, Singapore unilaterally imposed its own sanctions against Russia over the invasion. 

Stuglev said Moscow takes such restrictions into account when engaging with partners, although it does not recognise restrictions imposed by third countries.

“Practical cooperation makes sense where economic interest and clear regulatory frameworks coincide. We do not pretend that restrictions do not exist; they exist in the financial sphere and for certain categories of goods, and they have to be reckoned with,” he said.

Russian companies could also explore opportunities in transport and logistics connectivity, including the Northern Sea Route, energy and the deeper processing of raw materials.

Digital technology is among the more realistic areas for cooperation, he said, pointing to Russian expertise in cybersecurity, IoT applications and platform solutions that could potentially be adapted for Singapore and expanded across the Asia-Pacific.

Artificial intelligence could offer opportunities beyond technology exchange, including discussions on its ethical use and regulatory boundaries, he added.

Trade between Russia and Singapore amounted to US$4.5 billion (S$5.8 billion) in 2024, up 81% from 2022, while Russian exports grew by 90%, Stuglev said, citing figures he received from the Russian Ambassador to Singapore Nikolay Kudashev.

Energy supplies form the backbone of bilateral trade. Data for 2026 show that trade growth continues, he said. 

Russia’s trade with ASEAN amounted to US$4.8 billion in the first quarter, according to Russia’s Center for Foreign Trade under the Ministry of Industry and Trade. Singapore accounted for US$1.3 billion or 26% of total turnover, placing it second after Indonesia at US$1.4 billion.

In the first half of 2026, trade with ASEAN grew by almost 10% – or 58% over 10 years – to US$21 billion, according to Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development.

Stuglev said interest from South-East Asian businesses in Russia was also changing, with more companies attending major business forums on their own initiative instead of waiting for official visits.

However, companies operating in Russia continue to face practical difficulties involving payments, insurance, logistics and visa procedures, Stuglev acknowledged.

Roscongress has introduced services such as business-matching platforms, negotiation facilities, a mobile application and an investment catalogue to help participants navigate the process.

He invited Singapore businesses to attend the 30th St Petersburg International Economic Forum, which will be held from June 16 to 19, 2027.

Beyond commercial ties, Russia is also looking at cooperation in education, talent development and cultural exchanges, including academic competitions, university partnerships and professional training.

“In the sphere of education, sport and culture there should be no sanctions: this is a humanitarian area on which the development of both the region and the world as a whole depends,” he said.

He argued that international business forums remain relevant in a more fragmented geopolitical environment, as companies and countries seek avenues to maintain contact.

“Even competing blocs need a point where they can meet directly, because business is more pragmatic than politics,” he said.

data.title: AirAsia’s third-quarter loss narrows to $120m, but cash dwindles and liabilities rise
data.description:
Malaysian budget airline AirAsia on Nov 23 posted a net loss of RM381.3 million (S$119.8 million) for the third quarter, as elevated jet fuel prices and foreign exchange losses weighed on its operations.

The loss for the three months ended Sept 30 was much narrower than a net loss of RM830.5 million in the second quarter. The loss attributable to equity holders was RM175 million.

Revenue fell 8.4% to RM4.66 billion from RM5.09 billion in the prior quarter, as AirAsia trimmed capacity by 12% quarter-on-quarter amid fleet rationalisation. About 31% of its 234-strong fleet was out of service at the end of the quarter.

South-east Asia’s biggest budget carrier has said it is grappling with its most challenging financial period since the pandemic, after the Iran war led to a surge in jet fuel prices.

Foreign exchange remained a drag. AirAsia booked a net foreign exchange loss of RM141.9 million due to the depreciation of local currencies against the US dollar. No dividend was declared.

AirAsia did not provide year-earlier comparisons due to an accounting treatment arising from its January acquisition of the aviation business of affiliate Capital A.

Preparing for peak-season travel

AirAsia said it was “cautiously optimistic” that peak seasonal demand and fleet modernisation would strengthen its resilience heading into 2027. It said it was adding capacity on busy domestic and international routes to capture year-end demand.

It also said fourth-quarter fuel costs were still expected to be higher than in the third quarter despite a recent easing in jet fuel prices.

The airline reported cash and bank balances of RM905.3 million and current liabilities of RM19.2 billion as at Sept 30, compared to RM954 million and RM18.4 billion on June 30.

AirAsia controls about 60% of Malaysia’s domestic aviation market and employs about 26,000 people. Its stock has lost about 75% of its value in 2026.

The carrier has said it is aiming to raise up to US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) from international debt markets plus RM700 million in local credit facilities, primarily to refinance existing debt.

Co-founder Tony Fernandes said in October that he expected the fund-raising to be completed between December and February. The airline on Nov 23 gave no new fund-raising details, saying only that it was in “active engagements” with local and foreign financial institutions and progressing “liquidity-enhancing exercises”. REUTERS

data.title: China’s next AI deals clouded by sell-off after Anthropic IPO
data.description:
A sell-off in global stocks that has accelerated since the record US initial public offering of Anthropic is clouding the outlook for the next wave of share sales by China’s artificial intelligence champions.

DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and StepFun are among Anthropic’s direct competitors weighing or preparing share sales. While their plans do not hinge entirely on the performance of the Claude chatbot maker’s shares, the faltering global AI trade is adding complexity for the highly anticipated listings.

Their timing and pricing may also be impacted by investors having to contend with a changing regulatory backdrop and steep losses on earlier deals.

Anthropic’s US$119.5 billion (S$154 billion) deal became a catalyst for a scathing sell-off across AI stocks, triggering deep losses in several markets in Asia.

For China in particular, the trade that once made the country’s technology giants some of the world’s most coveted stocks has turned into a US$1.7 trillion rout.

The feverish pace of IPOs has slowed, and former standouts like Z.AI and CXMT have struggled.

“In the second half of 2026, the AI fever has cooled in midst of the market volatility, as investors focus more on return on investment,” said Thea Jamison, the New York-based managing director of Change Global Investment.

“The overall IPO market in China has abated, as both the China Securities Regulatory Commission and HK’s Securities and Futures Commission have asked banks and intermediaries to improve deal quality.”

AI fund-raising helped lift Hong Kong first-time share sale proceeds to a six-year high of US$52.3 billion, making 2026 the second-best year on record and putting 2010’s US$57.8 billion peak within sight. 

But some recent deals already showed how quickly AI euphoria can turn.

Z.AI and MiniMax Group were among the first generative AI firms to list in Hong Kong in January.

Shares of Z.AI plunged more than 85% from their June peak after soaring 2,000% in less than six months. Its smaller rival MiniMax broke below its issue price in November.

Anthropic’s first two days as a public company were a microcosm of the same dynamic after the company shattered records with its IPO and rose into the ranks of the most valuable in the world.

Its shares surged 17% from the offer price in their debut to give it a US$1.8 trillion fully diluted market value.

But they fell 8.5% on the second day of trading, swept up in a global sell-off that had the MSCI All Country World Index on course for its longest losing streak since September 2023.

Regardless of the market fluctuations, just having the market leader traded publicly – possibly followed by OpenAI in 2027 – can help the share sale plans of other model makers by setting benchmarks and helping investors understand their dynamics, said Kieron Poon, investment director of Asian equities at Aberdeen Investments.

“This better-than-fear valuation should give support to overall tech sector sentiment,” Poon said. “It also may foster OpenAI’s IPO process. After that, the market may have less concern about the transparency of annual recurring revenue among global LLM as their reporting standard will align further.”

The China Securities Regulatory Commission gave informal instructions to investment banks about pausing IPOs, the Financial Times reported in November, citing three unidentified people with knowledge of the discussions.

Kimi K3 developer Moonshot has closed a final private round at a valuation of about US$50 billion and is heading toward a Hong Kong IPO in the first quarter, seeking to raise as much as US$5 billion, people familiar have said.

DeepSeek is also eyeing a landmark listing in early 2027. The start-up was close to securing at least 80 billion yuan (S$15.4 billion) in its latest round, well above its initial 50 billion yuan target, people familiar said in October. 

Infinigence AI, a Shanghai-based AI cloud infrastructure provider backed by Tencent Holdings and Baidu, has filed confidentially for a Hong Kong listing that could come in the first half, Bloomberg reported.

Another Shanghai-based start-up, StepFun, is also considering raising about US$500 million.

“In the near term, I don’t anticipate the return of IPO fervour in China/Hong Kong until the market sentiment improves,” said Jamison. “That said, Moonshot AI’s IPO has been in the works and should be the most anticipated AI name in the near term.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Six workers file employment claims against Crystal Jade Food Manufacturing
data.description:
SINGAPORE – At least six individuals have filed employment claims against Crystal Jade Food Manufacturing, the company that operated the restaurant group’s central kitchen, amid a restructuring that saw the kitchen cease operations in October.

The claims come after Crystal Jade’s Singapore and Hong Kong holding companies were placed under receivership in September, followed by the closure of several restaurants and the issuance of termination notices to over 100 employees.

Court hearing records identified by The Straits Times show six cases against Crystal Jade Food Manufacturing, involving six separate claimants.

The Employment Claims Tribunals hears employment disputes involving salary-related claims and wrongful dismissals that have not been resolved through mediation.

The nature of the six claims, the amounts sought and whether they are directly related to the central kitchen’s closure have not been established.

In response to ST’s queries, Food, Drinks and Allied Workers Union (FDAWU) general secretary Sankaradass S. Chami said the union has been supporting members affected by the closure.

Although Crystal Jade is not unionised, FDAWU has been working with TADM@NTUC to help affected members understand the claims process and file employment-related claims for money owed under their employment contracts.

Following Crystal Jade’s communication with affected workers on Oct 7, the union also worked with NTUC’s Employment and Employability Institute to provide on-site assistance and connect workers with job opportunities.

“No worker should have to navigate work transitions alone,” Sankaradass said.

Central kitchen ceased operations on Oct 5

Crystal Jade Food Manufacturing’s central kitchen ceased operations on Oct 5, days after representatives from financial and risk advisory firm Kroll were appointed receivers over the group’s Singapore and Hong Kong holding companies on Sept 29.

Receivership is a process in which appointed professionals take control of certain company assets or businesses, typically to protect the interests of creditors.

Kroll previously said the central kitchen’s closure was a management decision and fell outside the scope of the receivership.

In its latest response to ST, Kroll reiterated that the closure was outside the receivership, but said management and the receivers had worked closely with unions to provide resources and opportunities for affected employees.

Kroll declined to comment on the latest status of the proposed sale of Crystal Jade’s Singapore business.

According to Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority records obtained on Nov 23, Crystal Jade Food Manufacturing was incorporated in 1997 and is wholly owned by Crystal Jade Culinary Concepts Holding, a company within the restaurant group’s corporate structure.

Despite the central kitchen’s closure, Crystal Jade Food Manufacturing remains registered as a live company.

4 outlets closed due to restructuring

The wider restructuring also saw four Crystal Jade restaurants close on Oct 6. They were three Crystal Jade La Mian Xiao Long Bao outlets at Bugis Junction, Toa Payoh and i12 Katong, and a Crystal Jade GO outlet at Oasis Terraces in Punggol.

Kroll said in October that about 120 employees working in the restaurants and certain corporate functions had been issued termination notices.

Following the closures, Crystal Jade had nine operating restaurants in Singapore and a workforce of about 210.

Kroll previously said the restructuring was intended to position the business for a proposed sale and support its long-term future.

ST has contacted the Ministry of Manpower for comment.

data.title: The Jensen Huang saga: What protections are there in Singapore from the cult of the founder-CEO?
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Jensen Huang’s sudden departure from Nvidia has left a huge leadership vacuum and thousands of shareholders in the lurch.

This should send a powerful message to boards and regulators everywhere, including Singapore: No company, however successful, should become so dependent on one individual that his or her unexpected departure threatens the company’s future.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and transformed it into one of the world’s most valuable companies, resigned as chief executive and director on Nov 12 after reports surfaced about his personal relationships and their potential security implications. Nvidia has appointed its chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief while searching for a permanent successor.

The issue is not Huang’s private life, nor is there any need to diminish his extraordinary achievements. Instead, it is whether Nvidia’s board had adequately prepared for the eventuality that the man synonymous with the company might suddenly become unavailable.

It is a question that should concern every shareholder, especially in Singapore, where dozens of listed companies are closely identified with the founders or are largely family-owned.

Founder-led companies often outperform precisely because their leader possess exceptional vision, determination and entrepreneurial instincts. However, outperformance can breed complacency and over-reliance on that individual.

The danger is that if a founder becomes larger than the company, directors may become reluctant to challenge decisions, senior executives may hesitate to disagree, and shareholders may place excessive faith in that founder’s judgement.

Stated differently the danger is that good corporate governance is sacrificed to a cult of personality.

In Nvidia’s case, reports indicate that Huang had at least 60 executives reporting directly to him but with no obvious successor publicly identified. This raises an uncomfortable question: How did the board exercise effective oversight when so much authority and institutional knowledge reside in only one person?

An independent board must be more than just a collection of rubber stampers who meet periodically to approve management proposals and collect directors’ fees.

Its fundamental responsibility is to protect the company and its shareholders – and this includes the consequences of excessive dependence on an exceptionally successful boss.

Hyflux: Singapore’s own cautionary tale

Singapore need not look overseas for lessons. Consider Hyflux, once celebrated as a homegrown success story with its charismatic founder Olivia Lum.

Lum was widely admired for building a water treatment business that became a beacon for Singaporean entrepreneurship. Her achievements attracted considerable public recognition and investor confidence, yet Hyflux eventually collapsed, unable to pay its debts and leaving thousands of shareholders and 34,000 holders of preference shares and perpetual securities with nothing.

Central to its difficulties was the Tuaspring integrated water and power project whose commercial viability depended heavily on electricity sales. When electricity prices fell sharply, so did the project’s viability.

With hindsight, it is reasonable to ask whether too much faith in the founder contributed significantly to insufficient scrutiny of the associated risks. Were directors sufficiently sceptical of management’s assumptions? Did they adequately challenge the company’s expansion into a new business area? Were shareholders properly told of the risks?

Hyflux illustrates a basic weakness that can arise in founder-dominated companies: When the founder’s reputation becomes a substitute for rigorous scrutiny, shareholders may pay a very high price.

Is Singapore’s governance framework sufficient?

In Singapore, the Code of Corporate Governance requires boards of companies listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) to establish nominating committees (NCs) responsible for reviewing succession plans for directors, the chairman, the chief executive, and key management personnel.

In addition, SGX’s practice guidance says that succession planning must ensure orderly replacement of board members and key management personnel, and this must include contingency planning “for preparedness against sudden and unforeseen changes”.

In practice, NCs generally interpret “sudden and unforeseen changes” to encompass any unexpected leadership vacuum, including:

The issue, therefore, is not the absence of rules but whether those rules are effectively observed by listcos.

A company can easily comply formally with succession-planning requirements without actually convincing shareholders that a credible successor really exists.

How many firms can confidently assure investors that they have someone capable of taking over tomorrow if their founder-CEO unexpectedly departs today?

How many NCs have genuinely tested their succession arrangements rather than simply placing a rubber stamp that says the matter has been duly discussed?

Perhaps companies, particularly those where the founder exercises substantial influence, should be required to disclose their succession and contingency plans, or at least whether potential successors have been identified and developed.

An interesting consideration is this: Where do companies stand on marital indiscretions or infidelities involving top management or charismatic founder-CEOs?

Should such transgressions, especially when they involve another staff member, lead to automatic dismissal or resignation?

Undoubtedly, this is a sensitive and complex issue, so perhaps it is best that all companies – not just those dominated by influential founders – discuss internally where they stand if and when key personnel succumb to temptations outside of marriage.

This will require consideration of the values that the company holds sacred and wishes to uphold.

True independence is crucial

The problem is that succession planning, however thorough, is not enough. It has to be complemented by independent directors who are genuinely prepared to challenge the status quo and prevent directorial groupthink from setting in.

Note that independence cannot be measured solely by the absence of family relationships, business dealings or other connections.

A director who has served alongside a powerful founder for many years may technically satisfy independence requirements yet find it psychologically difficult to question that founder’s decisions.

This is why periodic board renewal, independent evaluation and willingness to challenge major capital expenditure plans are essential. Independent directors must remember that their duty is owed to the company and its shareholders, and not to the founder who invited them to the board.

The Securities Investors Association (Singapore) (SIAS) stands ready to assist – but will have to take its cue from shareholders

For the past 27 years, SIAS has helped level the playing field for the minorities of dozens of companies in dealings with major shareholders and bigger counterparts through constructive engagement rather than outright confrontation.

It has been a fruitful approach, yielding many successes.

But as sound as this approach may be, legal action cannot be ruled out where serious governance lapses occur, or where directors refuse to address legitimate shareholder concerns, or where losses are due to actionable misconduct.

However, even though SIAS has raised succession issues with family-owned companies via its Three Questions for Annual General Meetings, it must be noted that the primary responsibility for questioning Boards must rest with shareholders and not necessarily SIAS.

It is incumbent on the true owners of a company’s capital to raise the issues discussed here, including substantive director independence, founder-CEO longevity or over-reliance, succession planning and contingency arrangements. This can be either at AGMs or through other channels mandated by listing rules.

Only when all these avenues have not borne fruit can SIAS enter the picture.

The ultimate test

The Jensen Huang episode should encourage regulators, directors and investors to reconsider the risks of over-dependence on charismatic corporate leaders.

The ultimate test of a well-governed company is not simply how brilliantly it performs under an outstanding leader but really whether it can continue to prosper when that leader is no longer at the helm.

Good governance means ensuring that the company is always bigger than the person running it. There are protections in place to ensure this, but they require all stakeholders to play their part.

data.title: World’s largest miner unveils US$17.4b plan to double South Australian copper output by 2040
data.description:
MELBOURNE – Top global miner BHP said on Nov 23 it plans to double its South Australian copper production by 2040, as it raises its exposure to the metal expected to drive electrification, with a final investment decision due in the first half of 2027.

BHP plans to spend between US$13.6 billion (S$17.5 billion) and US$17.4 billion to raise production to an estimated 650,000 tonnes a year from its sprawling copper operations in a remote region that it says is the world’s richest source of copper outside Chile.

The plan knits together its Copper South Australia operations at its anchor Olympic Dam copper mine, its Ankata deposit, and the mines gained in its A$9.6 billion (S$8.2 billion) purchase of OZ Minerals in 2023.

“We start from a strong position as the world’s largest copper producer, with a sector-leading growth pathway that can be funded from existing copper cash flows,” Geraldine Slattery, BHP’s head of Australian operations, told investors on a site tour, according to prepared remarks supplied by BHP.

“Copper South Australia is a centrepiece of that growth, contributing around a third of the increase to 2035.”

BHP projected Copper South Australia’s output would grow to rival its share in Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, by 2040. That would underpin BHP’s goal to produce 2 million tonnes of the metal, or 2.5 million including byproducts, from its global operations by the mid-2030s.

Slattery said BHP expects global copper demand to grow by 30% by 2040 to more than 45 million tonnes per year, driven by electrification, digitalisation and AI demand.

BHP, the world’s largest listed miner, reaped more value from its copper division than from iron ore, its prior mainstay, for the first time in fiscal 2026.

Challenging region

BHP has twice shelved plans in previous decades to develop its rich but technically complex ore assets, citing high costs and commodity downturns.

The operations have proven challenging due to a combination of operational instability, complex metallurgy and external infrastructure constraints such as water and power, UBS said in a note.

As a result, the operations have achieved a low single-digit return on capital employed for many years, reaching only 10% in fiscal 2026 with record-high commodity prices, UBS added.

BHP said it expects block caving, which is a type of bulk mining, and two-stage smelting to underpin significantly lower operating costs. It said phase one, which aims to produce 500,000 tonnes of copper annually by 2035, would have an internal rate of return of 14% to 17%, and capital intensity of US$18,000 to US$23,000 per tonne of copper.

As part of the expansion, BHP plans to roughly double the capacity of its uranium processing plant to 5,000 to 6,000 tonnes a year. It would also boost its gold production by 45% to more than 570,000 troy ounces a year.

Desalination options

BHP’s mines sit within the Gawler Craton, an ancient geological structure formed roughly two billion years ago, in an increasingly arid region on the fringes of Australia’s remote Outback.

The miner uses water from the Great Artesian Basin, which has sparked concerns about overuse from traditional owner groups such as the Arabana people. BHP aims to mitigate its use of the artesian water by using a planned 260-megalitre-a-day seawater desalination plant at Cape Hardy on South Australia’s Spencer Gulf. That water would need to be piped hundreds of kilometres.

The state government is running a tender for the multi-user Northern Water infrastructure project with two global consortia. It is due to make a final investment decision in 2027, and the first water from the project is targeted for fiscal 2032.

The planned expansion will also require power upgrades to existing electricity transmission infrastructure. REUTERS

data.title: E-mail blunder sees Australian bank NAB speed up job cut talks
data.description:
National Australia Bank (NAB) was forced to bring forward conversations with employees affected by planned layoffs, after it inadvertently told some staff they were being let go ahead of a formal communication.  

The bank had sent the e-mail on Nov 23 to staff who had already chosen to leave as part of a restructuring that had been recently announced, and were not intended to be sent before employees learnt directly about the outcome of the process, according to NAB. 

The message had notified them that their system access would be turned off on Dec 2, the Australian Financial Review reported earlier. The staff were meant to meet their managers this week to ascertain if they would still have a job or receive a payout, according to the publication.

“We are very sorry this happened, and that receiving an automated e-mail this way would be upsetting and unsettling to many,” NAB said. “This is not the experience we wanted any colleague to have, and we sincerely apologise for the distress this error has caused to any who received these e-mails.”

NAB is planning to cut up to 2,500 jobs as part of an overhaul to navigate heightened competition, a sluggish economy that has weakened home lending and rapid technological change, it said in October.

The process to exit workers has run into mishaps when firms botch the process. In 2025, rival ANZ Group Holdings had to accelerate planned layoffs after automated e-mails were mistakenly sent to some employees before they were told of their termination. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Around two-thirds of Singtel SDS holders choose to hold their shares as scheme concludes
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singaporeans who had bought Singtel special discounted shares (SDS) and left them in their CPF accounts will now be able to manage their shares directly through their Central Depository (CDP) accounts.

Singtel and the CPF Board announced on Nov 23 that they have completed the transfer of SDS on Nov 21. This ends the CPF Board’s legacy role as the trustee of the SDS.

Around 209,000 SDS holders, or 34%, had sold their Singtel SDS before the transfer. The rest of the SDS, amounting to 477 million held by about 406,000 holders, were transferred to their CDP accounts.

Around two-thirds of SDS holders who kept their shares already own individual CDP accounts, while the remaining one-third had their shares automatically transferred to designated CDP accounts created in their names.

SDS holders who also own Singtel ordinary shares will have both sets of shares consolidated in the same CDP accounts for ease of management, Singtel said.

The SDS scheme was introduced in 1993 as part of the Government’s efforts to give Singaporeans a stake in the Republic’s economic success through share ownership.

Singtel was the first and only company to offer SDS shares when it transitioned from a statutory board to a listed company that year.

The CPF Board was appointed as trustee to facilitate the share purchase, as share ownership was still a foreign concept among many Singaporeans at the time.

Today, with stock market trading ubiquitous, the SDS scheme has met its intent and the trustee arrangement to support share ownership is no longer necessary, CPF said in April, when the decision to end the scheme was announced.

SDS holders were thus allowed to sell their shares for cash or wait for their shares to be transferred.

According to Singtel data, the median Singtel SDS holder owns 1,360 shares at an average purchase cost of $2,000. At April’s market price of around $5 per Singtel share, those shares would have been worth about $6,800.

Parliament subsequently approved the CPF Amendment Bill in May to formalise the winding down of the scheme.

Singtel and the CPF Board advised SDS holders to remain vigilant against scams and to verify the URL of the SDS website to ensure it is the official one.

CPF monies withdrawn by members, including any SDS sale proceeds refunded to their Ordinary Accounts, will be credited to their bank accounts registered with the CPF Board.

If they suspect they have fallen for a scam involving their CPF savings, they should get their bank to freeze their bank accounts, reset their Singpass password, and activate the CPF Safety Switch to immediately cease any unintended monetary outflows.

Singtel group chief financial officer Arthur Lang said in a statement: “Over the past several months, our focus has been on ensuring SDS holders had the information, resources and support needed to navigate this transition with confidence, and we are pleased that the transfer has been completed smoothly.

“This initiative was ultimately about giving SDS holders a choice and enabling them to exercise their rights as shareholders directly.”

He added that Singtel now has greater flexibility to engage its shareholder base, execute corporate actions and allocate capital in ways that enhance growth and shareholder returns.

Singtel shares opened 1.4% lower at $4.11 when the market started trading on Nov 23. The telco’s shares have fallen around 17% since April.

data.title: Singapore’s core inflation eases to 1.5% in October
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore’s overall inflation dropped in October due to lower inflation for services, and electricity and gas, though with a slight increase for retail and other goods.

Core inflation year-on-year slowed to 1.5% compared with September’s 2%, according to data from the Singapore Department of Statistics on Nov 23. October’s core prices remain unchanged on a month-on-month basis. Core inflation excludes private transport and accommodation to better reflect household expenses.

Overall inflation year on year also fell to 1.9% in October from the previous month’s 2.2%, because of lower services, electricity and gas, and private transport inflation. On a month-on-month basis, it fell by 0.3% in October.

The speed of private transport inflation slowed to 6.7% from September’s 7.1% due to a more gradual increase in car prices, while accommodation inflation was unchanged at 0.9% in October as housing rents rose at a similar pace compared with the previous month.

Services inflation dropped to 1.1% from September’s 1.7%, due to smaller increases in airfares as well as in the costs of health insurance and healthcare services.

Retail and other goods’ inflation, however, picked up to 1.6% from 1.2% the previous month, as furniture prices rose and household appliance prices fell at a slower pace.

Food inflation shrank slightly to 2.3% from September’s 2.4%, due to the prices of non-cooked food rising at a slower pace.

Electricity and gas prices’ inflation had the biggest drop to 1%, from September’s 8.7%, due to electricity prices rising at a slower pace in October.

The decline in year-on-year electricity inflation was largely due to the lower regulated electricity tariff in October 2026 compared with that in September.

data.title: MSCI discussed avoiding Indonesia downgrade with Prabowo, Dalio
data.description:
MSCI chief executive Henry Fernandez conveyed a willingness to consider alternatives to a two-step downgrade of Indonesia’s stock-market status in recent direct talks with President Prabowo Subianto, according to people with knowledge of the discussion.

Fernandez and Prabowo spoke for more than an hour on a Nov 10 conference call brokered by Ray Dalio, the billionaire founder of hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing information that is private.

Dalio, who has acted as an informal adviser to Prabowo’s government, joined the call, as did Rosan Roeslani, the CEO of the Indonesian sovereign wealth fund Danantara. A few other minders and close aides were also dialed in, one of the people said.

Fernandez told participants that MSCI did not necessarily intend to downgrade Indonesia and instead would continue to advise Indonesian officials on the steps they would need to take to ensure they meet the necessary standards, the people said.

Those measures include removing people with political affiliations from the board of the country’s Financial Services Authority, which MSCI feels is conflicted and should be taking more robust action.

They also include improving communication with investors and providing clearer rules around issues such as the high shareholding concentration list, as well as the criteria and timing for changes to the LQ45, an index of 45 of Indonesia’s most liquid stocks, one of the people said.

Prabowo, for his part, pledged greater enforcement, another person said.

Spokespeople for MSCI did not respond to a request for comment. Indonesia’s Government Communication Agency and the Financial Services Authority also did not respond to requests for comment. Representatives for Dalio did not respond to a request for comment.

MSCI stunned investors globally in October when it threatened to strip Indonesia of its emerging-market status and push it down two rungs to standalone – an unusually severe step that went beyond its earlier warning of a downgrade to frontier market.

The index provider said on Oct 15 that reforms promised by Indonesian authorities had failed to produce sufficient, sustained improvements in a market dogged by opaque shareholding structures, suspected coordinated trading and weak enforcement. 

The move came after MSCI first raised the downgrade threat in January and, in June, gave Jakarta until its November review to show progress. MSCI in October said it is taking feedback until April 30 and plans a final decision by the end of June 2027.

A downgrade to standalone status would necessarily trigger billions of dollars in outflows as investors tracking MSCI indexes adjust their holdings.

A decision by MSCI to retain Indonesia’s emerging-market status would also support a currency that has fallen to record lows and lift a major overhang from Indonesian stocks. The local share market is among the world’s worst performers in 2026, down around 40%.

Dalio said he was also speaking on behalf of investors that viewed MSCI’s move as an overreaction, one of the people with knowledge of the conversation said. He named firms including JPMorgan Chase & Co, Goldman Sachs Group and Jane Street Group, the person added.

Representatives for JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs did not respond to requests for comment. Jane Street also did not respond to a request for comment.

Dalio, 77, is a longtime acquaintance of Fernandez and has met multiple times with the Prabowo administration in an advisory capacity, the people familiar said.

Days before Prabowo’s inauguration in October 2024, Dalio gave a virtual lecture to incoming Cabinet ministers who were attending a retreat at the president-elect’s private residence in the hills outside of Jakarta. Several months later, he became an unpaid, informal adviser to Danantara, which Prabowo created in early 2025 to oversee Indonesia’s state enterprises and manage state investments.

The cordial relationship has continued with Dalio meeting with Prabowo at the Presidential Palace in Jakarta in September 2025, after which he was awarded the Bintang Jasa Utama, or First Class Star of Service, a high-ranking civilian honour, in appreciation of his economic counsel and contributions to strengthening the Southeast Asian nation’s relations with the global financial community.

Dalio, in receiving the medal, said that it was a great pleasure “to be helpful and part of your mission”.

The president’s call with MSCI came three weeks after Prabowo said in a televised speech that Indonesia would not be intimidated by the US index provider, even as his regulators moved to crack down on misconduct in the stock market.

Officials in Indonesia have unveiled record fines against companies and brokerages related to market manipulation and introduced measures designed to improve ownership transparency and share availability in the nearly US$500 billion (S$645 billion) stock market. BLOOMBERG

data.title: US futures bounce as AI rout rattles Asian stocks
data.description:
SINGAPORE – US stock futures rose on Nov 23 while the authorities scrambled to shore up sliding stock markets in Asia, after a wipe-out last week for the tech and chip stocks at the centre of the AI boom.

Investors are questioning whether vast sums of mostly borrowed money spent building data centres to power AI tools will generate returns fast enough to repay lenders or big enough to justify some of the high stock prices.

Last week’s 10% drop in the Nasdaq was its largest weekly decline since pandemic panic gripped markets in March 2020 while the fall in Taiwan’s benchmark was the biggest since 1990.

Taiwan is home to the world’s dominant advanced chipmakers and critical link in the AI supply chain.

On Nov 23, Nasdaq 100 futures bounced nearly 3% in early trade and S&P 500 futures rose by 2%, while Taiwan stocks steadied and South Korean shares fell about 4% to a 10-month trough before finding support.

South Korea’s finance minister is due to hold a press conference later on Nov 23 about a potential market stabilisation fund, which was helping stave off further losses.

“We need to be a bit careful here,” said portfolio strategist Damien Boey at Wilson Asset Management in Sydney.

A suite of mood indicators he tracks showed US markets spent three sessions in “panic” territory last week, he said. That can sometimes signal the worst is over, but in this case there might not be enough momentum for the tide to turn.

“If you don’t have a policy pivot (at central banks) then there’s no catalyst for a risk appetite panic to turn into a durable bounce,” he said, leaving investors jumpy and unsure.

Japanese markets were closed for a holiday on Nov 23 but futures indicated selling pressure, while markets in Hong Kong and China sank to new multi-month lows.

The “AI trade” has for years lifted a wide range of stocks, from switch and cable makers to electricity generators, but they have all been under pressure in recent months from rising interest rates.

AI-related shares took a particularly sharp downturn last week as the exit of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive nicknamed the “godfather of AI”, and the faltering debut of AI company Anthropic, which closed 8.5% lower on its first full day of trading, pointed to a souring mood.

Taiwan’s financial regulator on Nov 21 ordered a further tightening of short-selling rules for stocks, while in China stock exchanges announced a batch of support measures such as easing requirements for margin financing. REUTERS
