data.title: Beijing to bar young ‘red-chip’ firms from listing outside mainland China, sources say
data.description:
China’s securities watchdog has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip firms to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said, a move that tightens its control of capital raised offshore and could dent Hong Kong’s IPO market.

Red-chip companies are registered abroad, mainly in tax havens, but control assets and businesses in China via equity ownership or contractual agreements.

The structure is favoured by Chinese start-ups, particularly tech firms, keen to raise capital in places like Hong Kong or New York to take advantage of more relaxed rules and deeper pools of funds available from foreign investors.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has told law firm representatives in recent days that red-chip companies established after the introduction of new offshore listing rules in 2023 must be re-domiciled in China before they can list offshore, said the people.

The people declined to be identified as the regulatory guidance was confidential. The move is being reported for the first time by Reuters.

China and the US are competing fiercely to gain the upper hand in tech, particularly in AI and semiconductors, which has led to efforts by Chinese authorities to sharpen their scrutiny of technology, data and capital going outside its borders.

The CSRC did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Oversight of red-chip firms has gradually become stricter.

Prior to March 2023, Chinese companies employing overseas holding structures to raise capital abroad did not need regulatory approval. That changed with the advent of the new rules.

Then this year, the CSRC told Reuters in March that it was examining the “necessity and compliance” of red-chip structures, particularly those formed after March 2023.

Despite that warning, some red-chip IPO hopefuls and their advisors have been seeking approval to list outside the mainland without dismantling their existing structure and shifting their domicile back to China, one of the people said.

Most of those applicants failed to convince the regulator that a red-chip structure was necessary, prompting the tougher stance, the person added.

Hong Kong IPO market could be hurt

A drop-off in listings from red-chip firms is likely to hurt but not hobble Hong Kong, the top IPO destination for Chinese firms, which has seen business boom for the past 18 months.

Funds raised via IPOs in Hong Kong during the first 10 months of this year surged 84% from the same period last year to hit HK$404 billion (S$66 billion), though the CSRC has slowed approvals of IPOs since September.

In addition to going slow on approvals for listings by AI, chip and humanoid robot firms after a market frenzy in those sectors, it has more broadly increased its scrutiny as markets have weakened.

In 2025, one-fifth of 131 Hong Kong listings approved by the CSRC involved offshore holdings, the majority of which used a red-chip structure, according to Chinese law firm Han Kun.

So far this year, the CSRC has approved Hong Kong listings for just 6 red-chip companies, a sharp decline from 50 approved in 2025, according to data compiled by law firms and Reuters.

There were nearly 600 listing applications pending in Hong Kong at the end of October, official data showed.

Most of them are mainland Chinese firms though it was not clear how many are red chips given that the number includes applications that were filed confidentially.

There are, however, at least four active Hong Kong IPO applicants which have an offshore holding company structure for their mainland China businesses, according to a Reuters review of filings with the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Any red-chip firms seeking to list in Hong Kong or New York could now face a long wait before coming to market due to the time and costs involved in becoming incorporated in China.

But some, like Chinese AI firm StepFun, have been working on shifting their domicile back to China to pave the way for a planned overseas listing, sources have said.

StepFun did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Asked about news of the ban on red-chip firms listing outside mainland China, the Hong Kong bourse said it “welcomes issuers with a range of ownership structures, provided they meet all applicable regulatory requirements in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions”. REUTERS

data.title: Gold rebounds as traders pare bets on near-term US Fed rate hikes
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Gold rebounded from its biggest weekly decline in eight months as traders scaled back bets on the Federal Reserve raising interest rates in the near term. 

Bullion rose as much as 1.3% to around US$3,582 an ounce, after falling 9% last week to a 14-month low.

Traders are paring expectations of monetary tightening after growing concerns about artificial intelligence spending rippled across markets, sending technology stocks plunging. 

Following the rout, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned the Fed risks jeopardising the US economy by overtightening in response to latest inflation data. His prior attempt to rein in elevated long-term borrowing costs sent yields lower in August, which sparked a brief rally in gold. 

Swaps traders are no longer fully pricing in a Fed rate hike in December after Treasury yields fell across the curve on Nov 20. The policy-sensitive two-year yields ended 12 basis points lower, a positive for non-yielding bullion. 

Gold has fallen by a around a third since the US-Iran war erupted in late February as higher energy costs fuelled inflation, prompting central banks to raise rates. It has traded below the US$4,000 support level since Nov 11.

Spot gold rose 1.1% to US$3,578.24 an ounce at 8.26am in Singapore, while silver was up 2.6% at US$42.21 after tumbling 15% the week before. Platinum and palladium also advanced. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index dipped 0.1% after rising 0.6% last week. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Procter & Gamble to increase factory shifts without humans to cut costs
data.description:
Consumer product giant Procter & Gamble says it plans to increase the number of factories that can run shifts without human intervention over the next several years as a way to increase productivity and save up to US$10 billion (S$13 billion).

The Cincinnati-based maker of Gillette razors, Tide Pods and Crest toothpaste has invested heavily in recent years in automated manufacturing lines that can run unattended for several hours at a time, often in the overnight hours.

P&G currently operates 15 such sites around the world and plans to add more in 2027.

“We are taking unattended operations to a whole new level,” Luc Reynaert, chief product supply officer, said on Nov 19 in a presentation to investors in Cincinnati.

Procter & Gamble has also deployed autonomous robots at loading docks and in warehouses, and has experimented with driverless trucks. Reynaert said unattended operations will improve manufacturing productivity by up to 20% over the next four years.

But the rise of so-called dark-shift manufacturing has provoked fears of enormous job losses. In a speech in June at the United Auto Workers quadrennial constitutional convention, the union’s president, Shawn Fain, called robots replacing humans in factories a “profound threat”.

Josh Bivens, chief economist at the Economic Policy Institute, a pro-labour think tank, said unattended factories were “not the thing that keeps me up at night”, because it’s difficult to stop automation once companies begin making upgrades.

He said the United States should increase its social safety net to better cover workers displaced by such technological advances.

Procter & Gamble had its first unattended shift at a Gillette factory in Berlin in 2024. The plant now runs without technicians during the hard-to-staff overnight shift, freeing up employees to focus on less-repetitive tasks or jobs in which they interact with customers during the day.

Procter & Gamble executives said unattended shifts give workers better schedules and allow them to focus on consumer-facing tasks, but acknowledged that they will need leaner teams.

On Nov 19, the company said it would cut its product-supply workforce, which includes contractors, by 20% to 30% by 2030.

Product-supply jobs at the company include roles in manufacturing, purchasing, planning, engineering and quality control. Roughly 65,000 workers fall into that category.

However, a company spokesperson said the reductions have been underway for a few years as part of a supply-chain improvement program called Supply 3.0. NYTIMES

data.title: ‘Size isn’t everything’: OCBC chief eyes higher ROE, bringing staff along even as bank grows
data.description:
SINGAPORE – For OCBC group chief executive Tan Teck Long, the struggles of small business owners hit close to home.

Growing up, his father ran a small business, but cash flow was often tight.

“As a micro business owner, when he made more money, he had to reinvest more. Even though it was profitable, we still did not see a lot of money in the household for luxury items or spending,” Tan told The Straits Times, adding that the business eventually folded.

His personal experience has shaped his concerns for small businesses, which align with OCBC’s longstanding commitment to supporting small- and medium-sized enterprises.

Beyond providing access to financing, OCBC supports SMEs with workforce training and business insights.

Its new partnership with NTUC LearningHub offers free courses for business owners and employees, while the OCBC SME Index tracks business activity and outlook across industries.

Despite his humble background, Tan did well enough in primary school to attend Chung Cheng High School (Main) and later Raffles Junior College.

He graduated with first class honours in accountancy from the National University of Singapore and later earned a master of business administration from the University of Manchester.

He spent nearly three decades at DBS Bank, where he began his career as a corporate banking trainee in 1993 and rose to hold several senior leadership positions, including group chief risk officer.

His time with DBS included a five-year stint leading DBS’ institutional banking business in China.

Tan joined OCBC in 2022 as head of global wholesale banking – overseeing relationships with SMEs, large corporates and financial institutions, alongside transaction and investment banking – before assuming the group CEO role in January 2026.

The 56-year-old is the first Singaporean to head OCBC in more than 25 years.

Under his watch, OCBC’s earnings grew in the first three quarters of 2026, underpinned by strong growth in wealth management.

Tan said OCBC’s key priorities are to grow, create value for investors, and execute its “next frontier” strategy, the growth road map unveiled in February under his leadership.

But, noting that “size is not everything”, he stressed: “We need to run the bank with higher return on equity, and we need to be steady in navigating the risk environment.”

Beyond becoming a bigger bank, he also considers how to bring staff along on the journey, saying, “that’s very important to me”.

The bank will continue to target the mass market alongside affluent and high-net-worth customers, with products and services catering to customers across all age groups.

He highlighted the bank’s entry-level investment products, including its blue chip investment plan and precious metals trading, which allow investors to start from as little as $100.

“We are taking care of the mass market customers in Singapore. We see that as a source of strength. We’re not going to give that up.”

To deepen engagement across its customer base and drive top-line growth, OCBC is leaning heavily into artificial intelligence, digital and data under its “next frontier” strategy.

In July, the bank launched what it called South-east Asia’s first AI-native mobile banking app, OCBC WoW. Featuring AI-powered avatars Wendy and Wayne, the platform provides customers with personalised wealth insights, portfolio analysis and investment ideas around the clock.

“We realise that relationship managers (RMs) have limitations. RMs, for example, cannot be there 24/7. So this is how we think about technology supplementing the RM,” Tan said.

By making financial advice more accessible, OCBC aims to encourage customers to invest and transact more, capturing a larger share of their wealth while freeing human advisers to handle more complex needs.

“An AI-native platform allows us to personalise the experience for customers. When you go on our website, everyone sees the same website. But avatar banking, over time, will be customised and bespoke to individual customers, so it’s more intuitive to customers’ needs.”

Still, Tan stressed that digital tools are meant to augment people rather than replace them, with the bank investing heavily in both technology and talent.

Training and development of RMs include a six-month generative AI-powered skills training programme to coach wealth advisers in a full range of competencies, including investment advisory, client management, product mastery and wealth planning.

At the same time, the bank is expanding its front-line workforce, hiring 600 additional RMs for its consumer banking business over the next three years. Its private banking arm, Bank of Singapore, is also adding hundreds more.

“We want to be known as a bank that can use technology to amplify customer relationships and staff capabilities,” said Tan, adding that the bank’s achievement will come not just from building the careers of its bankers, but also from finding the optimal mix of technology and people in serving customers and growing the franchise.

Even as OCBC pushes to harness AI, Tan made clear that the goal is not to spend blindly or engage in “token maxxing” – the practice of maximising AI token usage and treating sheer volume as proof of productivity.

“I have never set a KPI (key performance indicator) to say you must show me that you build more agents than the others. To me, burning tokens is burning money, so why go there?” he said, adding that OCBC’s token burn remains “very manageable”.

Rather than treating AI primarily as a cost-cutting tool, the bank views it as a lever for revenue growth through better customer service.

“The way we think about AI is different from many other companies. We don’t focus on cost efficiency only. If we get cost efficiency, we are very happy. The biggest opportunity is how to serve the customer better and how to get our revenue up,” said Tan.

That pragmatism also extends to choosing the right technology for the job, rather than deploying AI where simpler tools offer better returns. “For a bank that says we use AI when it’s fit for purpose, we prefer digitalisation. We prefer data because it’s always bang for the buck.”

Tan noted that geopolitical and regulatory uncertainty remains the biggest challenge facing businesses, driven by tightening US chip rules and ongoing conflicts.

New US curbs on chip exports have created uncertainty around compliance costs for data centre operators in South-east Asia, which could slow the pace of new deployments and weigh on clients.

However, Asia remains relatively insulated from the sharpest chip bottlenecks, he said. Unlike data centres built for heavy AI model training, most data centres in the region handle AI inference and everyday consumer workloads and therefore do not rely on restricted, high-end AI processors.

Meanwhile, prolonged conflicts in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine continue to threaten energy price stability. Those disruptions risk feeding into broader inflationary pressures, particularly food prices, requiring close, ongoing monitoring, he added.

data.title: Dreaming of a home, holidays and early retirement? Start with a monthly target: ST InvestMe panel
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Planning for a home, regular holidays and enough money to retire all at once can seem like a tall order but breaking each one down into a monthly saving target will make it easier to see what is affordable.

That was a key takeaway of a panel discussion on “funding your dream life” that was held on Nov 19 as part of The Straits Times’ InvestMe campaign, aimed at increasing the financial literacy of its subscribers.

Panellist Sheryl Choong, managing director and head of client advisory for Singapore at Endowus, said the starting point is to decide what a goal will cost and when the money will be needed. The time frame matters when choosing how to save or invest for it.

For instance, someone planning to buy and renovate a home within one to three years should consider less volatile options, such as a money market fund. With three to five years to prepare, they may be able to put more into fixed-income investments.

This is because money needed soon could be difficult to recover if the stock market falls just before a purchase.

The discussion, moderated by ST business correspondent Sue-Ann Tan, also explored whether young adults must choose between enjoying life now and preparing for the future.

She shared how she planned for her three trips to Europe in 2026 with a budget of $15,000 because she obtained good discounts by making all relevant bookings, including tickets to plays and concerts, about one year in advance.

Using this as an example, Choong said that those who have similar plans to spend $15,000 on travel annually should consider setting aside about $1,250 every month, for a year in advance.

But instead of splurging on multiple trips and work out the cost later, travellers can also start with an amount they can afford and adjust their plans accordingly.

Panellist Rosalind Ang, who is a business journalist at ST, shared how she and her husband made their first home purchase – an HDB resale flat – less daunting by planning to save for all the costs in stages.

The newlyweds reckoned that they also shaved about 50 per cent off their home renovation bill when they did their own research and doubled as the “designers” for their home.

They then picked a contractor and worked with its workers to implement the plans that they had drawn up.

Like many new home owners, Ang also shared how they bought many of their household items and even furniture online. But she had this piece of good advice: Never buy your beds online or you may end up sleeping on an uncomfortable choice for a long time.

The same approach applies to retirement, said Choong. People should work out the income they hope to have, take account of what they may receive from CPF Life, then assess what they need to save or invest to cover any gap.

That said, all three speakers agreed that it is not prudent for younger folk to pursue early retirement so aggressively that there is little time or money left to enjoy life along the way.

The Nov 19 event was the fourth in a series of six financial literacy courses. The final two will be held in January and March 2027.

To attend, readers can sign up for the ST InvestMe 24-month All Digital or All Digital and Print subscription package, which costs $29.90 per month.

Existing subscribers can recontract or upgrade their plans without incurring a penalty on their current plans.

Videos of earlier sessions are available on the InvestMe website, alongside practical financial tips. The site will also feature ST Invest columns and articles every weekend.

The next course, Real Or Not: Important Real Estate Tips by Invest editor Tan Ooi Boon, will cover property rules and changes that owners and investors should know. It will be held at the SPH Media auditorium in Toa Payoh North on the morning of Jan 16, 2027.

data.title: askST Jobs: My boss expects me to attend team bonding activities after regular working hours. Can I say no?
data.description:
In this series, business correspondent Timothy Goh offers practical answers to candid questions on navigating workplace challenges and getting ahead in your career. Get more tips by signing up to The Straits Times’ Headstart newsletter.

Is socialising with colleagues after work necessary to build good working relationships, or should doing one’s job be enough?

Doing one’s job well is important, but so is building good relationships with colleagues.

Socialising outside work can help colleagues get to know one another better, building trust and making it easier to communicate and work together, said Daryl Lim, chief executive of consulting firm AI-Thentic.

But employees should not feel pressured to attend after-work activities, as they may have personal commitments or prefer to keep their work and private lives separate.

“You do not have to attend every gathering, but joining colleagues occasionally, especially for important team events, shows that you value your working relationships,” Lim said.

“If you cannot attend, just explain the reason politely to your boss, and there is no need to share personal details or apologise excessively.”

Still, employees who regularly miss out on informal discussions where work decisions are made or information is shared may find themselves at a disadvantage.

In such cases, they could ask their manager about the purpose of these gatherings and suggest alternatives, such as a monthly team lunch during office hours.

Lim noted that meaningful workplace relationships can also be built through everyday interactions, such as conversations over lunch, coffee breaks or helping colleagues with their work.

“It starts with genuine curiosity, listening with empathy, appreciating different perspectives and being intentional about how we engage with others,” he said.

“What matters most is how well you work with others, not how often you join them for drinks or dinner.”

Chow Song Chee, a certified senior professional with the Institute for Human Resource Professionals, said employees may have legitimate reasons to decline after-work activities, including family responsibilities, personal commitments or simply needing time to recharge.

Respecting these boundaries should not be seen as a lack of team spirit or commitment to the organisation.

But employees should not assume that doing one’s job well is always enough to build strong working relationships.

“Workplaces run on relationships, not just responsibilities,” said Chow.

Technical competence and individual performance are important, but so are trust, camaraderie and mutual understanding, which help colleagues work together effectively.

“Informal interactions often create opportunities for colleagues to connect beyond their job titles, break down silos, strengthen psychological safety and develop the rapport that makes difficult conversations and cross-functional collaboration easier,” she added.

Still, there is a difference between encouraging employees to socialise and treating their participation as an unwritten measure of commitment.

“When attendance becomes an expectation rather than a choice, team bonding risks becoming performative,” said Chow.

“Such expectations could also disadvantage employees with caregiving responsibilities or different personal preferences. We should not confuse visibility at social events with actual workplace contribution.”

Managers should therefore create opportunities for employees to connect during working hours, through regular collaboration, open communication and inclusive team activities.

After-work gatherings can complement these efforts, but should not be a prerequisite for professional acceptance, recognition or career progression.

Employees should also recognise that building relationships requires effort, and making time to connect with colleagues occasionally can help strengthen trust and long-term collaboration.

“Employees have a responsibility to build constructive working relationships, but they should not have to surrender their personal boundaries to prove that they belong,” said Chow.

data.title: Anthropic’s post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
data.description:
Anthropic’s post-listing slide deepened the gloom over the AI sector on Nov 20, underscoring how even one of the most eagerly anticipated listings in history has struggled to revive investor enthusiasm.

Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain momentum after a turbulent stretch.

But the stock was last trading at US$88.87, about 9% below where it closed following its smooth debut on Nov 19, giving Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of about US$1.6 trillion (S$2 trillion) and a market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding.

The stock could find support later in the year. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30% of Anthropic’s shares by year-end.

Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

“We favour patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results,” said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation “assumes years of rapid growth”.

The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street’s main indexes ended sharply lower on Nov 19, while futures pointed to further declines on Nov 20.

Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia and Meta Platforms fell more than 2% each in premarket trading, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped more than 1%.

Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Sandisk down 7% each and Intel losing more than 5%.

The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which would be another major test of investors’ appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public in 2027.

Parallels with SpaceX

Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX , which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record.

While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.

“There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.

SpaceX shares fell about 5%.

Retail investors traded about US$772 million of Anthropic shares on Nov 19, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.

The stock’s sharp swings have left investors weighing whether to bet on a rebound or brace for further losses. Options trading, due to begin next week, could add to the volatility.

“It’s not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment,” said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg.

Competition could also weigh on investor sentiment.

Apple is developing an AI agent that can perform tasks on behalf of users, entering a market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, Bloomberg News reported on Nov 20. REUTERS

data.title: Oil prices gain as Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise supply concerns
data.description:
TOKYO – Oil prices edged higher on Nov 20, though set for a weekly decline, as concerns over supply disruptions grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude futures rose 59 US cents, or 0.6%, to US$92.57 a barrel by 0720 GMT (3.20pm Singapore time). US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures for December climbed 42 US cents, or 0.5%, to US$83.63 a barrel, while the more-active January contract gained 60 US cents, or 0.7%, to US$83.04.

Both benchmarks settled little changed on Nov 19, but Brent is set for a 3.5% decline for the week while the December WTI contract is set for a 6% weekly drop, as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. Brent and WTI are set to fall for the third week in a row.

“Concerns over Middle Eastern crude oil supplies have resurfaced due to attacks on Riyadh by the Houthis, prompting buying,” said Satoru Yoshida, a commodity analyst at Rakuten Securities.

“Expectations that coordinated production cuts will continue at the OPEC+ meeting later this month are also providing support,” he said.

The Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh, the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Iran-aligned movement.

Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and “exploded” and “are burning”, said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps Navy in a statement carried by state media on Nov 19.

Iran’s intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the waterway, “running at roughly one incident per day in November”, still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note.

OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on Nov 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia.

The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to the global oil and gas trade, and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Nov 19.

However, some analysts were still expecting softness in the broader equity markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Nov 20 – heading for their worst week since 2020.

“Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices,” said Saxo analysts in a note.

In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, Reuters reported on Nov 18.

Separately on Nov 19, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow would hit back hard after Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for a third time this week and said he was dropping any idea of a moratorium on attacking energy sectors and shipping. REUTERS

data.title: Anthropic’s post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
data.description:

As the first large machine-learning model maker to go public, Anthropic is widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, and its listing had been viewed as a potential boost for a sector struggling to regain its footing.

But the stock closed at US$88.91, 8.5% below the Nov 19 close and not far from its US$83 IPO price, while declines in other technology heavyweights suggested the listing had done little to stem the broader selloff.

“Anthropic faded relatively quickly. I don’t think investors believe there’s something inherently wrong with the company, management or business. I think they’re just skeptical of this market,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth.

The AI boom has come under pressure over the past month as concerns mount that spending on the technology, expected by some estimates to top US$1 trillion in 2026, is not generating returns quickly enough.

Fears of political hurdles to data centre construction and the leadership turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia have also added to those worries.

“Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds.

Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia fell about 14% and Meta Platforms dropped nearly 6%, Amazon lost about 4% and Microsoft ended3% lower.

Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Marvell Technology down about 13% and 12%, respectively, and Intel losing roughly 8%.

The focus now shifts to a potential listing by another AI leader, OpenAI, which could provide another test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year.

Despite a strong IPO pipeline of high-profile AI and infrastructure companies, many have pushed their IPO plans to 2027.

Patience may pay

Anthropic’s stock could find support in the coming weeks. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30% of Anthropic’s shares by year-end.

Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

But Morgan Stanley, the underwriter tasked with stabilizing Anthropic’s shares after its market debut, closed a position meant to do that, the company said, removing a potential pillar of support for shares.

“We favour patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results,” said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation “assumes years of rapid growth.”

The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street’s main indexes ended sharply lower on Thursday, while futures pointed to further declines on Nov 20.

Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX , whose June listing was the second-biggest on record.

Anthropic raised US$93.5 billion in its IPO after underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares, surpassing SpaceX’s US$85.7 billion haul to become the biggest listing on record.

While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.

“There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.

SpaceX shares fell close to 8%.

Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.

The stock’s sharp swings have left investors weighing the prospects of a rebound against further losses. Options trading, set to begin next week, could add to the volatility.

“It’s not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment,” said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg. REUTERS

data.title: Lufthansa to eliminate 1,000 jobs at struggling flagship airline
data.description:
Deutsche Lufthansa will cut 1,000 jobs at its namesake airline to turn around the unprofitable mainline unit, as high fuel costs put more pressure on Europe’s largest aviation group.

The company will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees seen by Bloomberg. Lufthansa Airlines also plans to further reduce capacity on short- and medium-haul routes and shrink its fleet of Airbus A320 aircraft, switching to the smaller A220 type, it said.

The planned reductions are the second culling in little over a year and reveal the extent of the struggles to revive the fortunes of the airline’s flagship product. The airline group announced in September 2025 that it intended to cut 4,000 administrative jobs by 2030.

Lufthansa is undergoing its biggest efficiency drive in years as high jet-fuel prices and an underperforming mainline airline weigh on results. Lufthansa Airlines posted an operating loss of €180 million (S$254.8 million) in the first nine months. 

“After two years of the turnaround, we have to acknowledge that the original measures are no longer sufficient to secure our future,” management wrote in the letter. “In fact, 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, persistently high fuel costs, nine days of strikes and our already very high cost base have made the situation more acute.” 

Lufthansa’s new supervisory board chairman, Johannes Teyssen, said earlier in 2026 that “significantly greater efforts” may be needed to improve the airline’s flagging performance after losing ground to rivals in what he called self-inflicted damage.

The measures revealed on Nov 20 come as Lufthansa tries to resolve a dispute with labour unions, though no agreement has been reached so far. BLOOMBERG
